headline: Fed Hike Talk Keeps Mortgage Rates Pinned Near 7.5%
tileReason: The daily 30-year average held at 7.51% Monday as lower oil prices offset more talk of Fed rate hikes; this morning's mixed retail sales and factory data left the 10-year yield near 5.13%.
takeaway:
Rates held steady Monday near their highest in over a month. The daily 30-year average edged up to 7.51% Monday from 7.50% Friday, essentially unchanged after three straight increases last week. Other trackers sit lower but moved the same way: Mortgage Research Center shows about 7.34% this morning and Zillow showed 7.39% Monday afternoon.

Lower oil prices helped bonds a little on Monday. Oil fell more than 3% Monday on signs that tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is recovering, and the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, slipped to about 5.12% from 5.15% Friday. A drop in stock prices also nudged some investors toward the safety of bonds.

Lenders didn't pass that small improvement along. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh spoke Monday about artificial intelligence and the economy but said nothing about interest rates or inflation, so his remarks didn't change expectations. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said inflation pressure is building but she isn't ready to back a faster pace of increases, which kept the mood cautious.

This morning's news was mixed. October retail sales rose 0.2%, and spending outside of car dealers rose 0.6%, stronger than the 0.4% expected; a sturdy shopper tends to push rates up. But industrial production, a measure of output at factories, mines and utilities, fell 0.4% when a small gain was expected, and oil is bouncing back after Monday's drop. The 10-year yield is about 5.12% to 5.15% this morning, close to where it ended Monday.

Fed officials keep talking about more increases. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said overnight the Fed likely needs several more rate hikes by spring to bring inflation under control. Futures markets, where traders bet on the Fed's next move, put the odds of a quarter-point hike in the Fed's short-term rate on Dec 9 at about 95% to 96%, with the rest on a bigger half-point move.

Lenders still have some cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.10% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 13, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond-market selloff.

The next tests come quickly. Nvidia reports earnings after the close today, and the minutes of the Fed's October meeting come Wednesday afternoon. After that: the Fed's preferred inflation measure on Nov 25, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via Trading and Investment News (Nov 17, 05:05 GMT); CME FedWatch via Reuters/The Star (Nov 16 close); Trading Economics (Nov 17)
fedOdds.note: These are the odds of a quarter-point hike. CME FedWatch showed 96.6% early Tuesday, easing to 95.7% by 05:05 GMT, with 4.3% on a half-point move, so a hike of some size is close to 100%. Reuters cited about 95% Monday, and Trading Economics shows nearly 95%. Monday morning's readings ranged from 91% to 94%.

drivers.title: Fed officials keep calling for more hikes
drivers.text: St. Louis Fed President Musalem said the Fed likely needs several more increases by spring, and futures markets put the odds of a December hike near 95% to 96%. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling.

drivers.title: Shoppers are still spending
drivers.text: October retail sales rose 0.2%, and spending outside car dealers rose 0.6%, above the 0.4% expected. A sturdy consumer gives the Fed less reason to ease up, which keeps upward pressure on yields.

drivers.title: Inflation still running hot
drivers.text: October consumer prices beat forecasts for the third month in a row, and wholesale prices are up 6.5% from a year ago. Bond investors demand higher yields when inflation eats into what their interest is worth, and mortgage rates follow.

drivers.title: Oil fell Monday and factory output slipped
drivers.text: Oil dropped more than 3% Monday on signs that shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is recovering, helping pull the 10-year yield down to about 5.12%. This morning, industrial production fell 0.4% versus a small expected gain. Cheaper energy and a softer economy tend to pull yields and mortgage rates down, though oil is bouncing back today.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.10% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 13, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields without raising rates as much.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 16 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even, with a slight lean higher. Mortgage rates have steadied near 7.5%, and the 10-year Treasury yield is holding just above 5.1%. Working against borrowers: a December Fed hike is close to fully expected, officials such as St. Louis Fed President Musalem are talking about several more increases by spring, inflation reports keep running hot and shoppers are still spending. In borrowers' favor: oil fell Monday, factory output slipped in October, stock prices are shaky, and mortgage rates still sit unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.10% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Big swing events: Wednesday's Fed minutes, the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision, Dec 10 consumer prices and oil headlines tied to Iran.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average held at 7.51% Monday, its highest in over a month but still below the 7.6%-plus levels of early October. Fed officials keep talking about more rate increases, and a December hike is close to certain, so the next few weeks could be bumpy. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates gave back most of October's improvement last week and are holding near 7.5%, and October home sales fell 5.5%, so buyers are feeling the pinch. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out heading into the holidays.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates are holding near 7.5% as Fed officials keep talking about more rate hikes and the 10-year Treasury yield stays above 5.1%.
